original_paraphrase: Israelite is a retrospective technical category. Location, settlement pattern, function, chronology and quantities jointly matter; a single jar or house type does not establish the occupants' identity.
chronology_basis: Iron I terminology; later monarchy used retrospectively

original_paraphrase: Regional field coverage and pottery chronology are uneven. Unclear older survey data are generally excluded; finer dates within Iron I remain difficult.
chronology_basis: Published and preliminary research through approximately 1985–1986

original_paraphrase: An exposed southern sector underlies the reconstruction of a peripheral house belt and central courtyard. The full ellipse and total house count are reconstructed.
chronology_basis: Late 11th century attribution in source; not a complete excavated perimeter

original_paraphrase: Imports, public buildings, copperworking, size and discontinuity distinguish Masos from small hill villages. Finkelstein disputes its use as a generic Israelite settlement model.
fact_interpretation: compiled excavation findings plus author interpretation
chronology_basis: Strata III–I chronologies disputed; no first-century implication

original_paraphrase: Pottery rechecking from more than half the previously proposed Iron I desert sites produced no diagnostic Iron I pieces. This revises the earlier classification but does not supply complete regional detection.
chronology_basis: Surface diagnostics; absence of diagnostic sherds is qualified

original_paraphrase: Pottery in fills may be residual, adjacent silo outlines can be confused with cuts, and a partial silo can be constructed against a wall. Shape and fill alone cannot securely fix a silo's construction phase.
chronology_basis: Iron I and 10th-century phases debated

original_paraphrase: Fortress reconstructions and historical owners changed between reports. Missing clean floor assemblages, sections and levels prevent the surviving corner from fixing a complete fortress and fine chronology.
fact_interpretation: compiled excavation evidence and author critique
chronology_basis: Chronology and function unresolved in source

original_paraphrase: Necropolis pottery establishes activity more securely than the muddled wall and rock-cut phases. A small exposure and contradictory assignment of early/late walls leave Iron I fortification uncertain.
chronology_basis: Cemetery evidence distinguished from settlement construction

original_paraphrase: A composite plan includes remains of several periods. The chronology of individual silos cannot be recovered from the total plan; the storage comparison expressly assumes, for argument, their simultaneous Iron I use.
fact_interpretation: compiled plan plus explicit author assumption
chronology_basis: Iron I through Persian architecture; silo cuts individually undated

original_paraphrase: A single-phase settlement has bonded pillared houses and a substantial 2–3 m outer wall. Its historical connection to Philistine pressure is inferred, and the schematic plan follows the first excavation season.
fact_interpretation: reported field observation and author historical inference
chronology_basis: Late 11th to late 10th century site occupation in source

original_paraphrase: Contiguous rear rooms form an outer belt. Interpretations of blocked alleys and silo changes as an ethnic population replacement are challenged.
fact_interpretation: compiled excavation plan and author interpretation
chronology_basis: Iron I; exact historically fixed foundation dates disputed

original_paraphrase: The alphabet ostracon was recovered from silo 605, but Finkelstein states it need not belong to Stratum II. Its recovery locus alone does not date the silo's original construction.
fact_interpretation: excavation context with explicit phase caution
chronology_basis: Iron I artifact; construction/use/fill distinguished

original_paraphrase: Plans document an enclosure, central stone construction, ash/bone material and installations. The altar, ramp and supratribal center are Zertal's reconstruction; Finkelstein discusses competing explanations and dating difficulties.
chronology_basis: Two Iron I phases; scarab and ceramic dates qualified

original_paraphrase: The six-site pithos table comes from oral excavator communications. A proposed sequence of Galilean before Tyrian pithoi is explicitly left for statistical and future field validation.
chronology_basis: No independently established regional sequence supplied

original_paraphrase: Mittmann's Plain of Irbid/Ajlun comparison separates terrain units and period counts. Publication was incomplete and the timing relative to Canaanite centers remained unresolved.
chronology_basis: Late Bronze, Iron I and Iron II classifications

original_paraphrase: The project revisited mapped sites and older Iron I collections, using diagnostic pottery. Sparse early activity can still be missed, especially beneath later village occupation.
fact_interpretation: author field method and detection limitation
chronology_basis: Survey counts throughsummer 1987; no complete detection guarantee

original_paraphrase: Site area describes the entire ruin, not necessarily its Iron I extent. Water distance is the straight-line distance to the nearest permanent source. Cisterns were reported at every site; later installations were largely deferred to the final survey publication.
chronology_basis: Whole-site and surface information; cistern construction dates not supplied

original_paraphrase: Sherds occur on broad terraces near caves. Medieval shepherds used the caves as a seasonal campsite; the earlier pottery scatter does not date the caves' cutting or establish an early cave function.
fact_interpretation: surface observation and stated later use
chronology_basis: Middle Bronze and Iron I sherds; medieval cave use

original_paraphrase: A large multi-period ruin contains cisterns, quarrying and burial caves. The entry does not assign each visible feature a construction date.
chronology_basis: Many periods represented; individual feature phase unknown

original_paraphrase: The catalogue places the 30 dunam ruin on a ridge in a wadi and lists 50 m to the nearest permanent water source. It cites A. Mazar 1982 a, Had. Arch.76(1981):19 and Kallai 1972:172; this entry supplies no pool construction date.
fact_interpretation: catalogue field context and bibliography route
chronology_basis: Iron I village classification; water feature construction unknown

original_paraphrase: Sixteen threshing floors lie south of the sheikh's tomb and medieval ruin. The photo locates them in the present landscape but the entry does not phase all floors.
chronology_basis: Iron I/II/Hellenistic pottery; medieval remains separately identified

original_paraphrase: Two winepresses and two cisterns lie near a covered building beside a small valley. A single Iron I sherd occurs among Iron II, Roman and Byzantine pottery; individual installations remain undated.
chronology_basis: Mixed-period site; feature chronology unknown

original_paraphrase: Pits on the neighboring hilltop are compared with the Gibeon winery. The proposed Iron I settlement on its eastern slope is tentative; the comparison does not establish a pit's date or original function.
chronology_basis: Mixed-period ruin; pits not phase-isolated

original_paraphrase: The ruin has a kind of crypt with loculi in the north and cisterns in the west, with reused stones and a massive terrace wall. The entry gives multi-period pottery without dating those cuts.
chronology_basis: Iron I/II and Byzantine sherds; construction unknown

original_paraphrase: Iron I sherds were found only in a stored Department of Antiquities box; the current survey did not itself recover that evidence. A. Mazar's Late Bronze collection is an oral communication.
chronology_basis: Pottery reports distinguished from securely phased architecture

original_paraphrase: Population is estimated from inhabited area at 25 persons/dunam. Early Iron I areas are arbitrarily assumed to be half their later size; pastoralists without visible remains are omitted.
chronology_basis: Iron I estimate; not a census

original_paraphrase: Permanent-water distance distributions are broadly similar for Middle Bronze and early/late Iron I. The diagram's points are not ordered by catalogue site, and it gives no date for a particular cistern.
chronology_basis: Period grouping from diagnostic sherds; water distances not hydraulic phases

original_paraphrase: Earlier occupation on western slopes leads Finkelstein to infer terracing before Iron I. The argument concerns ecological necessity; it does not directly excavate or date every terrace wall.
chronology_basis: Middle Bronze antecedent proposed; individual walls require independent dating

original_paraphrase: The source reports a large spring 900 m northeast of the tell supplementing collected runoff in cisterns. It combines topography, historical descriptions and name survival in identifying Shiloh.
fact_interpretation: field geography plus historical name/route tradition
chronology_basis: Mound spans many periods; spring/cistern construction dates not given here

original_paraphrase: Middle Bronze IIB pottery was incorporated in later IIC construction fills. Exposed wall/glacis and northern storerooms are distinct from the reconstructed full circuit and proposed sanctuary.
chronology_basis: Fill pottery earlier than construction; sanctuary unexposed

original_paraphrase: Pottery and bones occur in an accumulation without associated architecture. The proposed offering deposit and later dumping in Iron I are interpretations of that material.
chronology_basis: Object chronology versus redeposition distinguished

original_paraphrase: The separate excavation areas were not stratigraphically linked, so contemporaneity of their Iron I remains was not established. The Area D floor reused the top of a Middle Bronze wall.
chronology_basis: Iron I; multiple possible phases

original_paraphrase: A rock-hewn plastered cistern lay in the courtyard. The east entrance and access to basement 306 are reconstructed; a later massive wall and Byzantine kiln prevented verification of the route and steps.
chronology_basis: Iron I building context; cutting/plaster independently undated

original_paraphrase: Figure 69 is a schematic plan containing Middle Bronze, Iron I and Roman/Byzantine elements. Figure 70 is explicitly an isometric reconstruction; drawn openings and stairs are not all observed remains.
chronology_basis: Different construction phases shown together

original_paraphrase: Fourteen stone-lined Area D silos cut Late Bronze debris, two containing carbonized wheat. Cultic fragments above brick collapse and stamped jar material in the southern dump have depositional contexts distinct from the destroyed floors.
chronology_basis: Iron I silos; older substrate and later overlying debris

original_paraphrase: A summit sanctuary is favored through building organization, debris and exclusion of other areas. Its architecture was not exposed, and later construction badly damaged the summit/southern slope.
chronology_basis: Iron I religious center model; no independently surveyed sanctuary footprint

original_paraphrase: Silo plans combine cuts made across the life of a phase; not all need be contemporaneous. Izbet Sartah capacity extrapolates 43 excavated silos to 110, while Nasbeh comparison expressly assumes undated cuts in Iron I.
chronology_basis: Use/fill and construction dates distinguished

original_paraphrase: Diverse rims coexist at Shiloh. Very large stationary jars could survive beyond the end of their manufacture, so a later destruction assemblage does not provide a precise production date.
fact_interpretation: artifact context and author dating caution
chronology_basis: Mainly 12th–11th century; later survival possible

original_paraphrase: Complete jars in the conflagration lacked carbonized grain, while wheat occurred in silos and raisins near jars. Storage of liquids is inferred from these contexts and regional distribution.
chronology_basis: Iron I use contexts; exact former jar contents unknown

original_paraphrase: The 40,650 sedentary estimate at known sites becomes an author-corrected maximum near 55,000. Regional coverage, uncertain ethnicity, omitted pastoralists and sites occupied during only part of Iron I limit it.
chronology_basis: Iron I/around 1000 BCE horizon; not first-century population

original_paraphrase: Finkelstein proposes nomadization after Middle Bronze village decline and resedentarization as grain exchange weakened. Sanctuaries, cemeteries and modern analogies are indirect clues; causes and timing remain qualified.
chronology_basis: Ancient period sequence; modern ethnography remains analogy

original_paraphrase: The bibliography supplies original report and survey routes. Reading these entries does not constitute inspection of every cited publication; forthcoming works and unpublished census/inventory data retain that status.
chronology_basis: Citation dates through 1987; underlying sources separately required
